doc.title: Scott Yanow interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021

title: Jazz writers he admired and today's critics
summary: His early heroes were Leonard Feather, Hentoff, Stanley Dance, Balliett and Morgenstern; today Giddins and Francis Davis are highly rated.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Has there been a period of years for whatever reason jazz journalism and authorship was more difficult than others?

In the older days, say oh 1970 or so, there were less recordings coming out and there were less reviews to write. But then again you had some really tremendous writers, you know, some of the ones who I read when I was starting out were just great. And they all had their faults and their good points, but I mean my early heroes were Leonard Feather because he was so dominant during that era, even though you know he’s not perfect and there are certain things — I could talk about him for an hour. Leonard Feather, Nat Hentoff, and Stanley Dance who even though he hated bebop he was great when he talked about swing. You know he interviewed all these people, and Whitney Balliet I discovered after a little while, who was just a poetic writer, and the last, the only one really that’s still with us is Dan Morgenstern. I read him early on. And all three were

giants. We now have a lot more writers I think but there’s no one that dominates the field. You know Garry Giddins is great, you know he’s my generation. He and Francis Davis, you know, I rate them both very high. The current writers, also are quite good, I just can’t think of any one that I would pick out and see oh he’s the best one or she’s the best one right now.
